title: Enforcement, speeds and new risks: priorities for the Road Safety Strategy
label: 11 November 2026 · Road Safety Strategy evidence session
summary: Police, local highway and insurers’ representatives told the Transport Committee that the Government’s casualty-reduction targets won’t be met without more and better enforcement, clearer local speed rules, faster data-sharing and new rules for micromobility. They outlined gaps in funding, coordination and tools, and highlighted rising harms from illegal e-bikes, uninsured drivers and social-media-fuelled dangerous driving.

chapters.title: Targets need stronger enforcement and funding
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses agreed casualty targets are unlikely to be met without more enforcement capacity, better tools and extra funding.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are the Government's casualty-reduction targets achievable without a big increase in enforcement?

turns.speaker: Paul Fermer
turns.text: Short answer: no. Enforcement matters and needs to be the right type, but it's not the only element—we also need funding and community measures like Speedwatch.

turns.speaker: Angus Eaton
turns.text: I agree enforcement is fundamental. It must be modernised; some penalties are outdated and the people and bodies who can enforce may need to change.

turns.speaker: Joy Allen
turns.text: Yes. Also, different Government departments could pool effort and money: road safety saves lives and reduces costs across health, policing and social services, so joint funding makes sense.

chapters.title: Where to focus: speeds, rural roads and local limits
chapters.takeaway: Lower urban and many rural speed limits, plus clearer national rules, were proposed to reduce deaths and injuries.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You said the strategy underplays safe speeds and roads—can you expand?

turns.speaker: Paul Fermer
turns.text: Oxfordshire pushed 20 mph in many urban areas and saw benefits. We want 20 mph as the norm in communities and to reduce many A and B roads to 50 mph. It should be harder to justify higher limits.

turns.speaker: Angus Eaton
turns.text: Speed limits must match the changing vehicle mix, especially new micromobility devices. Limits alone won’t help if those vehicles aren’t regulated or enforced.

turns.speaker: Paul Fermer
turns.text: There’s confusion when different areas set different limits and satnavs disagree. A clearer national approach to default limits would reduce genuine confusion and non-compliance.

chapters.title: Data, partnerships and practical capacity gaps
chapters.takeaway: Better data sharing, record-keeping and joined-up local partnerships are needed so enforcement can be targeted and preventative.

turns.speaker: Alex Mayer
turns.text: What blocks effective joint working between police, DVLA and local authorities?

turns.speaker: Joy Allen
turns.text: Data sharing. We also don’t record many non-serious collisions that show local danger. If minor crashes and near-misses were reported they’d give a fuller picture for prevention.

turns.speaker: Angus Eaton
turns.text: Agree on data. Better, faster linking of insurance, MOT and tax data would help enforcement and predict problems. We also need legislative time for reforms.

turns.speaker: Paul Fermer
turns.text: Partnerships work, but priorities and funding differ across police force areas. Councils lost road-safety capacity and are rebuilding it; police and councils need matched resource.

turns.speaker: Joe Morris
turns.text: Does the system have enough officers to enforce current laws?

turns.speaker: Joy Allen
turns.text: No. Roads policing is much reduced from a decade ago. But we can work smarter—Sweden keeps roads policing part of every officer's shift—and use partnerships and education better.

turns.speaker: Angus Eaton
turns.text: It isn’t just officer numbers—it's tools. Initiatives like Tutelage, which bring data together to prioritise enforcement, need funding so police can be effective.

chapters.title: Enforcement tools: cameras, signage and uninsured driving
chapters.takeaway: Average-speed cameras, better national rules on signage, and real-time insurance data would improve compliance and reduce harm.

turns.speaker: Joe Morris
turns.text: How effective is the current system for enforcing speed limits?

turns.speaker: Joy Allen
turns.text: A mix exists: fixed cameras, average-speed cameras and community Speedwatch. They work where used, but they need capital, deployment in the highest-risk spots and supporting police capacity.

turns.speaker: Paul Fermer
turns.text: Average-speed camera programmes, like in Wales, change behaviour across a route better than single fixed cameras. But rollout is inconsistent and costly signs add maintenance overheads.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Does inconsistent local policy create sign clutter and extra cost?

turns.speaker: Paul Fermer
turns.text: Yes. Non-default limits mean extra signs and upkeep. We tried to minimise costs by using existing poles, but patchy signage can also make enforcement harder.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: On uninsured driving, how big is the problem?

turns.speaker: Angus Eaton
turns.text: Uninsured driving costs the economy ~£1bn a year; the Bureau pays ~£260m annually in claims. Reserves for illegal or modified e-bike claims have jumped markedly and fuel continuing pressure.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: Could real-time checks help the police spot uninsured vehicles?

turns.speaker: Angus Eaton
turns.text: Yes. We need faster, less stale data so officers can check insurance at the roadside. The industry and agencies are working on it, but it will take time.

turns.speaker: Joy Allen
turns.text: There are also grey areas: cars sold for parts or delivered unroadworthy can end up driven uninsured. Better responsibilities and data could close that gap.

chapters.title: Emerging threats: social media, micromobility and next steps
chapters.takeaway: Social-media-fuelled dangerous driving, illegal modified e-bikes and unregulated micromobility are rising harms that need regulation, faster penalties and education.

turns.speaker: Jacob Collier
turns.text: How big an issue is dangerous driving pushed by social media?

turns.speaker: Joy Allen
turns.text: It’s significant. People post high-speed or dangerous clips that others imitate; social media companies should take down content that facilitates crime quickly.

turns.speaker: Angus Eaton
turns.text: We’re seeing a surge in claims from illegal or modified e-bikes; reserves have risen from £30m to £128m. Regulation of these vehicles would allow insurance and reduce harm.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: Do education programmes work and could insurers require courses to reduce premiums?

turns.speaker: Angus Eaton
turns.text: Education is effective and targeted programmes help. Insurers could consider behavioural rewards, but lowering premiums directly via education needs careful evidence.

turns.speaker: Paul Fermer
turns.text: Beyond education, culture and ownership matter—drivers must recognise that getting in a vehicle means responsibility. Technology in vehicles could also limit speed if legislated.

turns.speaker: Joy Allen
turns.text: My final ask: a fully funded delivery plan with clear accountability so PCCs, councils and police know who does what and have the resources to hit the targets.

turns.speaker: Angus Eaton
turns.text: Regulate micromobility and be ready to review rules regularly. New vehicle types and offending patterns will keep emerging.

turns.speaker: Paul Fermer
turns.text: Require local highway and police authorities to adopt a Vision Zero approach and publish clear local speed-limit principles so national intent meets local delivery.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. If there’s anything you want to add in writing, please do so; the Committee will continue this inquiry.
